name: Hawthorne effect
statement: People are said to change their behaviour because they know they are being studied, an effect named after lighting experiments whose recovered data do not show it.
meaning: The claim is about the act of measurement rather than about any treatment. If a worker, a patient or a doctor behaves differently while a researcher watches, the measured effect of an intervention contains the effect of the watching. Control groups do not remove it, because controls are observed too. That is why the idea travels beyond psychology into trial design: a bias in the instrument matters everywhere the instrument is used. The label carries a stronger story with it, that output at the Hawthorne Works rose whatever the experimenters did to the lights. This entry is mostly about what happened when somebody read those data.

origin.who: Fritz J. Roethlisberger and William J. Dickson
origin.where: the book Management and the Worker (Harvard University Press)
origin.note: The studies came first and the name came later. Western Electric and the National Research Council planned the illumination work in November 1924, and Roethlisberger and Dickson date its end to April 1927, two and a half years. Elton Mayo joined as a consultant in 1928 for the second series, which Levitt and List say ran until June 1932. Roethlisberger and Dickson report the relay assembly test room only for its first thirteen periods, 1927 to 1929, and note that the room itself ran five years and that T. N. Whitehead analysed the whole of it in The Industrial Worker in 1938. McCambridge, Witton and Elbourne date the term's first use to 1953, in John R. P. French's chapter 'Experiments in field settings' in Festinger and Katz's Research Methods in the Behavioral Sciences. Wickström and Bendix name the same source and quote French on 'a marked increase in production related only to special social position and social treatment'.

evidence: The illumination experiments ran from 1924 to 1927 under two Western Electric engineers, George Pennock and Clarence Stoll, working with the National Research Council committee. Three departments of women inspecting parts, assembling relays and winding coils had their light varied and their output counted. Roethlisberger and Dickson quote the committee's own man, C. E. Snow, on what came out. In the first experiment the intensities were 3, 6, 14 and 23 foot-candles in one department, 5, 12, 25 and 44 in the second, and 10, 16, 27 and 46 in the third. Output there 'bobbed up and down without direct relation to the amount of illumination'. The second experiment gave a test group 24, 46 and 70 foot-candles against a control held near 16 to 28, and both rose by almost identical amounts. The third took the test group from 10 foot-candles down to 3 in one-candle steps, and both groups improved until the operatives protested at 3 that they could not see. Two operators were then moved to a locker room that could be blacked out and worked at 0.06 of a foot-candle, about moonlight, without losing efficiency. In a further test an electrician swapped bulbs for bulbs of the same size while the women watched, and their production 'did not materially change at any stage'. Levitt and List worked from the archived series instead. They describe a baseline of 4 foot-candles with manipulations up to 36, and a final phase with the windows taped black in which light was stepped down to 1.4 foot-candles for a single day. Changes were made on Mondays, because Sunday was the only day the factory was idle, and workers were told when a new period began. These data were never formally analysed at the time. The relay assembly test room that followed held six women, five assembling and a sixth laying out work, and was built by inviting two experienced operators to pick the rest. Operators 1A and 2A were transferred out for talking too much and replaced early in Period VIII. The popular account, which Levitt and List quote from textbooks, holds that every change in light raised output, including the changes that darkened the room.

replication.headline: The original illumination records were found again in three archives and the famous pattern is not in them, while two meta-analyses of purpose-built tests find a pooled effect that fades in the better-designed studies.
replication.detail: Levitt and List traced the illumination records to a microfiche room in a Milwaukee library and a second archive in Boston, and report that existing descriptions of supposedly remarkable data patterns 'prove to be entirely fictional'. Output in the first year rose to about 10 percent above baseline in all three rooms, against a plant-wide rise they estimate at 1.4 percent per worker per year. Output rises sharply on the Mondays when the light was changed, and an identical rise appears on Mondays when nothing was changed. What drives the raw data is the working week: Saturday output is very low and Monday output lower than other weekdays. Their regressions find no significant immediate response to a lighting change, the point estimate being negative on the day and positive the day after. Output ran 3 to 4 percent higher while experimentation was active, and that result disappears once room-by-month and month-by-year interactions are added. Artificial light entered positively and natural light negatively, and the artificial-light coefficient reached significance in only one of the two specifications. A one-standard-deviation change in artificial light moved output by under one percent. Those last two weak results are what Levitt and List call their strongest evidence of a Hawthorne effect. Izawa, French and Hedge found copies of the illumination documentation at Cornell and analysed it separately. They report an effect of lighting on productivity in the first treatment sequence of the first experiment, and no confirmation of it in the second sequence or in the second and third experiments. All three experiments, they conclude, were seriously flawed. Jones had earlier reanalysed the original data and concluded that they show 'slender or no evidence of a Hawthorne effect', in Wickström and Bendix's reproduction of him. Wickström and Bendix make the prior point that the illumination studies cannot carry the concept at all, because their results were never reported. Of the four studies that followed, they count one, the relay assembly test room, whose results have been attributed to the effect. Their recommendation is to drop the term and name the psychological and social variables a study left unmonitored. The modern methodological question is separate. McCambridge, Witton and Elbourne reviewed 19 purposively designed studies: 8 randomised trials, 5 quasi-experimental studies and 6 observational ones. Twelve of the 19 found an effect at conventional significance. Across the 14 studies with binary outcomes the pooled odds ratio was 1.17 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.30), with I-squared of 93.3 percent. The five trials alone gave 1.06 (95% CI 0.98 to 1.14), and the four observational studies gave the largest estimate at 1.29. Berkhout and colleagues repeated the exercise on work published from January 2012 to March 2022, checked for overlap with the earlier review, and pooled 15 reports from primary care and outpatient settings. Their overall odds ratio was 1.41 (95% CI 1.13 to 1.75), with I-squared of 97 percent. By design it was 1.08 (95% CI 0.98 to 1.19) in six randomised trials, 1.19 (95% CI 0.99 to 1.44) in four quasi-experimental or post-hoc analyses, and 1.80 (95% CI 1.22 to 2.66) in five observational studies. By level of evidence it was 1.04 (95% CI 0.99 to 1.09) in the eight high or moderate studies and 1.79 (95% CI 1.27 to 2.50) in the seven low ones. Both reviews put the signal in the weaker designs. McCarney and colleagues randomised the amount of observation directly, inside a Ginkgo biloba trial for mild to moderate dementia. They randomised 176 people to intensive or minimal follow-up and had cognition data on 140. Intensive follow-up came out ahead on the ADAS-Cog, mean difference -2.018 (95% CI -3.914 to -0.121, p = 0.037), and behind on participant-rated quality of life, mean difference -1.382 (95% CI -2.642 to -0.122, p = 0.032), with no difference on carer-rated quality of life. They had not powered the study for that comparison and call what they found a small effect. Abelleyra Lastoria and colleagues searched to August 2024 and found 28 wearable-technology studies that addressed the effect at all: 21 mentioned it, 4 tried to reduce it, and 3 tried to use it.

study.cite: McCambridge, J., Witton, J., & Elbourne, D. R. (2014). Systematic review of the Hawthorne effect: New concepts are needed to study research participation effects. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 67(3), 267-277.

replicated.weighting: DerSimonian and Laird random-effects pooling of the 14 included studies with binary outcomes, not weighted by study design

limits: The Levitt and List figures on this page were read off their NBER working paper, which is the version available in full, while the citation names the published article in American Economic Journal: Applied Economics. The publisher's PDF returned a login page to this machine, so any figure here should be checked against the published version before it is relied on. No effect size can be quoted for the original. Levitt and List say the illumination data were presented graphically and that they extracted them from the graphs; Izawa, French and Hedge took theirs from the tables and graphs in the archived reports. Jones's 1992 paper could not be obtained: the University of Chicago Press page returned HTTP 403 and the Semantic Scholar record carries no abstract, so his conclusion appears here at one remove through Wickström and Bendix. Roethlisberger and Dickson report the relay assembly test room only for its first thirteen periods, and two of its five assemblers were swapped out partway through. Both pooled odds ratios cover binary outcomes only. McCambridge and colleagues call theirs an 'apples and oranges' review, and heterogeneity at 93.3 percent says those numbers are not estimating one quantity. The manipulation is being interviewed in one study, filling in a questionnaire in another, and being watched washing one's hands in a third. Almost every included study sits in health sciences. Berkhout and colleagues attribute their own heterogeneity to the observational and low-evidence studies, and their review is confined to primary care, outpatient clinics and healthy subjects. Most of the observed effects are short-lived, and McCambridge and colleagues found them contingent on task and context rather than constant. Wickström and Bendix argue for retiring the term rather than for a finding about it, and their paper is a commentary, not a reanalysis of data. Levitt and List are careful that their own positive results are weak, and they leave open whether the higher output during experimentation reflects observation or something their controls miss.
misreadings: The claim that output rose whichever way the lights were moved is the part with no support in the data, and it is the part everyone repeats. The founding text does not say it either. Snow's first experiment has output bobbing up and down with no relation to the light, and in the sham bulb-change test production did not materially change at any stage. The piece of the story that does hold is the pair of operators who kept their rate up at 0.06 of a foot-candle. The Heisenberg comparison is a second misreading. Levitt and List note that the Hawthorne effect, unlike the uncertainty principle, is not guaranteed and depends on features of the setting. French introduced the name in 1953, long after the research, so 'what Mayo showed' and 'the Hawthorne effect' are two claims rather than one. The most common working use of the term, in McCambridge and colleagues' judgement, is as an after-the-fact reading of unexpected findings, above all null results in trials. Being watched is also not the same as knowing what the watcher expects, which is the observer-expectancy effect at entry 136 and the subject-expectancy effect at entry 268, nor the same as a belief about a person altering that person, which is the Pygmalion effect at entry 9 and self-fulfilling prophecy at entry 44.
